title: Mosopelea (Ofo) & the Ohio Valley
summary: Before the Shawnee dominated the Ohio hunting grounds, the Siouan-speaking Mosopelea, later called the Ofo, held eight villages north of the Ohio River.
bodyMarkdown:
The Mosopelea, later known as the Ofo, were a Native American people who once lived near the upper Ohio River. [An account of the Mosopelea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosopelea) says they moved south to the lower Mississippi in the late 17th century, after Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) invasions aimed at controlling hunting grounds. Their story shows that the Ohio Valley had a long Native history before the Shawnee and the Anglo-American settlers who came later.

## Eight villages north of the Ohio

A 1684 French map by Jean-Baptiste-Louis Franquelin shows eight Mosopelea villages just north of the Ohio River. They stood between the Muskingum and Scioto rivers, in what is now Ohio. Franquelin marked those villages as "destroyed."

The people also left a mark on the map's biggest river. The Miami-Illinois name Mosopeleacipi, meaning "river of the Mosopelea," referred to the Ohio. Shortened in Shawnee, the name became "Pelisipi" or "Pellissippi," which was later applied to the Clinch River in Virginia and Tennessee.

## War and flight

The French explorer La Salle recorded that the Mosopelea were among the peoples conquered by the Seneca and other Haudenosaunee nations in the early 1670s. Those attacks were part of the later [Beaver Wars](/stories/iroquois-beaver-wars/), a long struggle over the fur trade and hunting lands. Another people of the same era, the [Moneton](/stories/moneton/), appear only briefly in colonial records.

By 1673, Marquette, Joliet and other French explorers found that the Mosopelea had likely left Ohio and moved down the Mississippi. They lived for a short time with the Quapaw before joining the Tunica, who were allied with the French.

## On the lower Mississippi

French Jesuits met the Ofo living among the Tunica in 1699 and called them the Houspé. Around 1700, French travelers reported Ofo villages on the Yazoo River in Mississippi. The Ofo refused to join the Natchez in their wars against the French in the 1710s and 1720s and moved farther south.

Over time the Ofo and other small groups merged into the Tunica and Biloxi communities. Ofo families still lived among the Tunica in the 19th century.

## A language recovered

[An article on the Ofo language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ofo_language) says early linguists guessed that Ofo was a Muskogean language. In 1908 the anthropologist John R. Swanton met Rosa Pierrette, an elder who had spoken Ofo as a child. Her knowledge let him show that Ofo was a Siouan-Catawban language, close to Biloxi. The last known speaker died in 1915, and the language is now extinct.

## Kentucky today

The Mosopelea villages stood north of the Ohio, but the river that bordered Kentucky once carried their name. Ofo descendants remain part of the Tunica-Biloxi Indian Tribe, which has a reservation in Avoyelles Parish, Louisiana. The U.S. Department of the Interior has recognized that tribe as the successor of the historical Tunica, Ofo and Avoyel peoples and part of the Biloxi.
